## Function

CDH1 encodes **E-cadherin**, a calcium-dependent adhesion protein central to epithelial adherens junctions. Its cytoplasmic partners connect cell–cell adhesion to the actin cytoskeleton and intersect with β-catenin biology.

::: {.gene-mechanism}
::: {.gene-state}
**E-cadherin at junctions**

Epithelial cells maintain cohesion, polarity, and organized tissue boundaries.
:::
::: {.gene-flow-arrow}
→
:::
::: {.gene-state .gene-state-off}
**CDH1 reduced or lost**

Adhesion weakens; motility, invasion, and epithelial plasticity may increase.
:::
:::

In inflamed colon, junction disruption can arise without CDH1 promoter methylation, and bulk expression can change with epithelial loss. In neoplasia, CDH1 silencing may cooperate with many other alterations; it is not sufficient by itself.

## Evidence in colitis-associated neoplasia

In a small study of 14 UC-associated and 14 sporadic colorectal cancers, CDH1 promoter hypermethylation occurred in 57% and 36%, respectively, and methylation correlated with reduced E-cadherin protein [@wheeler2001cdh1]. A separate UC colectomy series found CDH1 methylation higher in actively inflamed than paired quiescent mucosa, with active inflammation remaining associated after multivariable analysis [@saito2011ucmethylation]. Together these studies support both inflammation-linked field change and cancer-associated silencing, but their small, selected tissue cohorts do not establish prospective predictive performance.

## Why localization matters

Total E-cadherin abundance can look preserved while the protein is internalized or displaced from lateral junctions. An informative assay should therefore combine exact promoter CpGs with epithelial-cell RNA, membrane-localized protein, β-catenin distribution, and permeability—not methylation alone.

<details><summary><strong>Best evidence chain</strong></summary>

Promoter DMR → lower CDH1 RNA → reduced/mislocalized E-cadherin protein → altered junction and permeability phenotype, all in the same relevant cells.
</details>
